articles.title: Albania’s protests show no signs of backing down
articles.author: Ana Vračar
articles.content: The months-long protests in Albania have reached a new escalation, with university students strengthening their mobilization since mid-October. Concerns about study expenses, poor employment prospects, and low wages have added impetus to a movement that has demanded the resignation of Prime Minister Edi Rama and urgent action on the widespread corruption weighing on the country. “Students have brought the Flamingo Revolution into a new phase,” wrote the Solidarity Albania platform. “In a capital where living costs devour 170% of the median net wage, public universities are starved to force youth into economic exile.” “When a generation rises for its basic rights, the only legitimate response is total solidarity,” they added. “Tirana’s struggle stands shoulder-to-shoulder with student strikes in France and India, and with liberation struggles in Palestine, Sudan, and the Congo, and elsewhere.” Police violence brings comparisons to protests in France Mass mobilizations against elite tourism projects, the devastation of Albania’s natural resources, and corruption have been ongoing since May this year – evolving in what was dubbed the Flamingo Revolution. For the past months, demonstrations have continued on a daily basis, Enriko Peçuli from the progressive party Lëvizja Bashkë told BreakThrough News . “Some days you saw more people on the streets, sometimes a bit less, but gatherings continued basically every night: the energy was there.” On October 13, when the latest upsurge began, “you could sense in the city that something was going to happen,” Peçuli adds. When students assembled in large numbers near the Ministry of Education and part of the building caught fire, police violence erupted, Peçuli says – and has continued for ten days in a row. Read more: Protests banned and curfews declared ahead of next major mobilization in France The authorities’ violent response has drawn comparisons to the institutional response to youth mobilizations in France, yet it represents a new element in local mobilizations. During other significant demonstrations, including the student protests in 2018, it was not as pronounced, Peçuli says – possibly indicating Rama’s worsening position. Ever since the beginning of the protests, the prime minister has tried to deflect responsibility and avoided the protesters’ core demand: his resignation. When the Flamingo Revolution started, Peçuli describes, Rama tried to blame it on foreign powers. He has named the governments of Greece, Iran, and Russia as culprits for the mobilizations. “It’s only gotten worse with time,” the activist points out. “He’s becoming more and more arrogant, he uses a language of violence.” “Rage is pushing people into the streets” After the escalation of the past days, Rama attempted – in a way – to establish dialogue with the students. This was resolutely rejected, as Peçuli notes that protesters will not agree to anything less than the government’s resignation. “It’s spontaneous rage pushing people into the streets,” he said, nodding to the events’ decentralized character that some have credited for at least part of the demonstrations’ longevity. “We don’t have trade unions or big student movements [like the ones in France], society is generally not organized in the same way,” Peçuli points out – but there’s no sign of backing down. “Rama might have offered dialogue, but it’s difficult to take that seriously after the past 10 days. After you’ve sanctioned breaking people’s heads, your right to call for dialogue is a bit limited.”

articles.title: Protests against electoral fraud continue in India
articles.author: Abdul Rahman
articles.content: Thousands of protesters marched to the headquarters of the Election Commission of India (ECI) in Delhi and to other government offices in several cities across India on Friday, October 23, as part of the ongoing nationwide demonstrations against alleged electoral fraud and manipulations. Protesters in Delhi carrying the national flag shouted slogans against the election fraud and the attacks on people’s right to vote, right to protest, and basic democracy in the country. They were stopped by the security forces deployed in large numbers who had barricaded all the routes leading to the ECI office hours before the protests began. Some of the protesters were also detained. Similar protests were held across different parts of the country on Friday and earlier this week . The protests in Delhi were called by People Against SIR, a group of over 300 organizations formed recently to coordinate ongoing protests. The group includes major trade and farmers unions, student and youth movements, and other sections of civil society. A large number of farmers also participated in the protests which have been ongoing since the beginning of the month and are expected to intensify in the coming days as all opposition parties and civil society groups have already called for a large demonstration in Delhi on November 1 over the failure of the government to respond to their demands so far. The march on Friday was converted to a public meeting after it was stopped by the security forces. Several people addressed the protesters, pointing out the complete disregard to the basic rights of citizens by the Narendra Modi-led government. Some of them also questioned the legitimacy of the ultra-right-wing government, claiming it was a result of a stolen mandate. Undeclared emergency The Narendra Modi government has imposed an undeclared emergency in the country by making it an offense to wave the national flag, arresting activists, and letting the police and pro-regime thugs repeatedly attack protesters, women and journalists, People Against SIR said in a press release on Thursday. The failure of the constitutional institutions, including the Supreme Court of India to intervene against the blatant misuse of state power and their failure to protect the basic rights of the people confirms the state of democracy in the country, it underlined. Two leaders of the CJP were sent to seven days of judicial custody after they tried to unfurl the national flag in central Delhi last week in an attempt to resist the government’s clampdown on the protesters. Hundreds of people, mostly young activists, have been detained, and beaten by the security forces since the beginning of the protests. Several of the women protesters and journalists have complained about police and pro-government thugs molesting and beating them during the protests. The government has repeatedly used sections of the law to restrict movement and barricaded the central parts of the capital city for weeks now. India cannot be allowed to become a police state The protesters decried the restrictions imposed by the government against protests in the capital and other places, calling it a violation of the right to peaceful protest. They announced that they will not let India become a “police state.” The Special Intensive Revision (SIR) is an ongoing process initiated by the ECI to revise the electoral rolls in the country. The opposition has alleged that the process was illegal and was initiated with the intention to manipulate elections to benefit the ruling ultra-right-wing Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), which has been in power since 2014. Several reports in the local newspapers have also claimed the Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar violated established legal procedures and made changes in the SIR process arbitrarily on several occasions to benefit the ruling party. Over 130 million voters, around 14% of all registered electorates in the country as per the 2024 data, have been removed from India’s decentralized electoral rolls since the process began last year. In some states a quarter to half of all electorates were removed. The number is significant especially given the fact that in India’s First Past the Post system, the victory margins in elections are often very small. Some have claimed that many of the voters removed from the roll were from religious minority communities or sections of the working class which have generally voted against the BJP. One of the major demands of the ongoing protests is the removal of the SIR process altogether. Protesters have also demanded the removal of the sitting CEC and for legal action to be taken against him, as well as the re-inclusion of all the people whose names have been removed from the electoral rolls.

articles.title: Miko Peled: ‘Israel is collapsing from within’
articles.author: Rania Khalek
articles.content: Benjamin Netanyahu will almost certainly stay as prime minister after Israel’s elections on Tuesday, Miko Peled predicts – but he argues it won’t really matter if he doesn’t. The Israeli-American author, activist and founder of Palestine House of Freedom in Washington, DC tells Rania Khalek and Zoe Alexandra who wins control of Knesset doesn’t really change things for Palestinians in Gaza and the West Bank; with challengers like Gadi Eisenkot, the ex-army chief behind the Dahiya doctrine of flattening civilian neighborhoods, and ex-premier and settlement champ Naftali Bennett who vows to block a Palestinian state, the war machine stays the same. But Peled says the ultra-Orthodox fight over the military draft and growing demands for an October 7 investigation are tearing Israeli society apart. He explains why settler attacks on Washington Post photographer Heidi Levine and Congressional candidate (and liberal zionist) Brad Lander show the state’s true face, pointing out “it’s all settler violence, because they’re all settlers.” Peled warns that a new Israeli attack on Iran could finally test the limits of Tehran’s restraint – and that if Netanyahu falls, Democrats may rush to re-embrace Israel ahead of the midterms, but the honeymoon won’t last. articles.title: Protests banned and curfews declared ahead of next major mobilization in France
articles.author: Ana Vračar
articles.content: Hundreds of thousands are set to take to the streets in cities across France on Saturday, October 24, once again protesting austerity and the cost of living crisis. Demonstrations are set to go ahead despite an extremely repressive response from the government and local authorities, including curfews and bans . Over the past couple of days, a growing number of cities and regions have announced protest bans, drawing criticism from trade unions and progressive groups. “The government has banned demonstrations on Saturday in Lyon, Marseille, Rouen, Grenoble, Le Havre, Bourg-en-Bresse, Le Mans, Toulon, Chambéry, Perpignan,” wrote Clémence Guetté of La France Insoumise on October 22. “New bans are coming down every hour. Is this what democracy looks like?” Many of the bans are being contested in court, with the final outcome yet to be determined. Read more: Italian government to deploy troops to Milan after anti-austerity protests French President Emmanuel Macron failed to revise his stance on the protests in the same period, announcing that only trade union mobilizations will be allowed on Saturday. “Where they are not organized by trade unions, we will ban them wherever we can,” Macron stated. The government announced the intention of deploying troops to “guard” the demonstrations. The idea was announced after nationwide protests on October 17 – attended by roughly 800,000 people – turned into riots against the erosion of education services and overall living standards . A securitization strategy tested in Kanaky This institutional response has been heavily criticized by progressive forces that joined students on the streets. As Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu’s administration insisted on framing the mobilization exclusively as a security issue, including in meetings with political parties, left forces denounced the strategy for failing to address concrete issues. Paul Vannier of La France Insoumise said the government was engaging in “a strategy of letting the situation rot,” insisting that it should instead shape a solution to students’ demands. This would include freezing prices, increasing wages, making higher education more accessible, and allocating €10 billion for the education system. Read more: Students in France are fighting for stronger public education The French left has also sounded the alarm about the long-term consequences of the violent repression of the protests: thousands of youth were arrested during the mobilization, and dozens were injured – some of them very seriously. While alarming, this course of events is not surprising, La France Insoumise pointed out. The party compared the repression observed in French cities to the one witnessed during protests in Kanaky in 2024: “a state of emergency, extended curfews, a general ban on demonstrations, the blocking of TikTok, nearly 3,000 security personnel deployed with army support, armored vehicles, and the massive use of LBD launchers and grenades.” “What the state tested in 2024 in Kanaky, it is now applying in 2026 to its own youth, with the same men in charge,” the media outlet L’Insoumission wrote. Trade unions’ support continues It is in this context that progressive forces in France have reiterated calls for the public to respond to the students’ call and protect their right to protest on Saturday. “On October 24, we once again call on all activists to put on their red [trade union] vests so that young people and workers can exercise their right to demonstrate and to make their demands heard,” the General Confederation of Labour (CGT) wrote. Students, trade unions, and progressive groups are mobilizing against austerity, the cost of living crisis, and eroding conditions in education. Source: CGT/Facebook “We are witnessing an authoritarian shift that goes hand in hand with the government’s stubborn refusal to own up to its record and to call into question its unjust policy in favor of the wealthiest,” dozens of trade unionists, advocates, and cultural workers wrote in an appeal , calling for support for the protests. “This choice is irresponsible and dangerous for democracy, and for the physical integrity of those who defend it without the framework of these mobilizations,” they stated. “It paves the way for the far right to come to power.”

articles.title: Kenyan Communist leader Booker Omole acquitted on all counts
articles.author: Nicholas Mwangi
articles.content: Booker Ngesa Omole, general secretary of the Communist Party Marxist–Kenya (CPM-K), has been acquitted by the Mavoko Law Courts in Machakos County, ending a prosecution that the party has described as politically motivated since his arrest in February 2026. In a statement issued on October 22, the party’s Central Organizing Committee welcomed the ruling as a victory for democratic rights and called for accountability over what it described as Omole’s abduction, torture, and political persecution. Speaking outside the court after the ruling, Omole said the verdict confirmed the party’s position that the charges against him were intended to target his political activities. “With finality, the court sitting today at Mavoko Law Courts has clearly indicted the current Ruto regime,” he said. “It has corroborated what we have told the Kenyan public, that framed-up charges against politicians and revolutionaries cannot endure in any competent court.” Omole said the judiciary had a responsibility to act as a check on state power and defend “the people’s democracy and freedom.” He accused the state of using criminal proceedings to pursue political opponents, adding that it “continues to fail to indict us on criminal charges but wants to persecute us politically.” “The acquittal is not for Booker only,” he said. “It is for the Communist Party and for all other people who want change in this country. I did not go to jail for nothing. I went to jail to make a statement, and today we prosecuted the case both in the court of public opinion and in Mavoko Law Courts.” From arrest to acquittal According to the party’s statement, Omole was abducted by armed men in plain clothes in Isiolo on February 24, 2026, and transported towards Nairobi before being detained at Mlolongo Police Station. The party says that he was tortured while in custody, sustaining injuries to his arm and tooth, as well as cuts to his fingers. The party further alleges that Omole was detained for more than four days before subsequent court proceedings and his eventual release on bail. He faced criminal allegations involving firearms, ammunition, drugs, and assaults against police officers. The prosecution case was subsequently weakened after the complainant and a prosecution witness, submitted a sworn affidavit on March 9 seeking to withdraw his complaint and earlier statements. The court acquitted Omole on all counts on October 16, 2026. It also ordered the immediate return of the party’s property held by police, according to the Central Organizing Committee. The acquittal brings the criminal proceedings against Omole to an end, but the party says it will continue pursuing accountability for the events surrounding his arrest and detention. Party demands investigation and accountability In its statement, CPM-K called for an independent investigation into the alleged abduction and torture, as well as the conduct of the police officers involved. The party also demanded full compliance with the court order to return its seized property and called for an end to what it describes as the criminalization of communist and revolutionary political activity. “The court has acquitted our General Secretary. The state must now answer for what was done to him,” the statement declared. CPM-K argued that the case should be understood within the broader political and economic conditions confronting Kenya, accusing the government of using state institutions to intimidate those organizing workers, poor peasants, students, and other oppressed groups. The party said the acquittal would not end its political activities or its demands for accountability. Instead, it called on its supporters and international communist and workers’ organizations to intensify solidarity efforts and defend democratic freedoms. Read more: CPM-K officials survive assassination attempt in Kenya Omole has faced threats and arrests before. In April 2025, a car carrying him and other activists was shot at. In September 2024, he was arrested during a wider crackdown on leftist activists. He also survived an assassination attempt on his life while at his residence last year.

articles.title: Ohio Governor’s Race: Trump Backs Ramaswamy Ad Siding with Opponent’s Indicted Childhood Rapist
articles.content: This is a rush transcript. Copy may not be in its final form. AMY GOODMAN : In the Ohio governor’s race, an attack ad has set off a firestorm of criticism from Democrats and many Republicans. Republican gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy, a tech billionaire, says he will spend $4 million more to promote the ad ahead of the midterm elections, even though it’s drawn criticism from members of his own party. The ad features his Democratic opponent Dr. Amy Acton’s estranged mother, in which she denies her daughter was sexually abused as a child. This is a brief clip. DONNA ARTHUR : I love my daughter, but when I saw her lying about her opponent, it’s not easy for a mother to say this, but Amy has a serious problem. AMY GOODMAN : The ad first began circulating on social media earlier this week. Dr. Acton responded to her mother’s appearance in the ad in a statement, saying, quote, “Between the ages of 10 and 12, I was sexually abused by her husband, while my birth mother did nothing to protect me. … My birth mother’s husband was arrested, charged with rape, and indicted by a grand jury. At 12 years old, I testified in court. I haven’t seen my birth mother since that day in 1978. She and her husband fled the state and he was declared a fugitive,” she wrote. Dr. Acton also addressed the ad in a campaign stop Wednesday evening. DR. AMY ACTON : But I’ve never attacked his family. I would never do that. This is despicable, what he’s done. And, you know, you can see that there are so many people who have experienced trauma and abuse in their lives. I’m running for governor because I won’t look the other way while bad actors, special interests keep taking my state backwards on nearly every single measure. AMY GOODMAN : Ohio’s Republican Senator Jon Husted, who’s in a tight race against Democratic candidate Sherrod Brown, the former senator, said he would not have run the ad. And Ohio’s current governor, Republican Mike DeWine, condemned the ad, calling it “wrong.” This audio is a bit rough, but listen carefully. GOV . MIKE DEWINE : It’s wrong to run this ad. And even at this late time, my wife Fran saw the ad run this morning on TV. I would just urge the Ramaswamy campaign to take this down. AMY GOODMAN : But also on Wednesday, Vice President and former Ohio Senator JD Vance said he’d been left feeling “disgusted” — not by Ramaswamy’s ad, but by Republican pushback against it. VICE PRESIDENT JD VANCE : I’m a little bit disgusted when I see Republicans across the country who are whining more about that advertisement than they are about what the congressional Democrats and other Democrats want to do to the United States of America. AMY GOODMAN : Meanwhile, President Trump has been fiercely defending the ad repeatedly on the campaign trail in Iowa, saying he advised Ramaswamy not to take it down, but instead to thank God. PRESIDENT DONALD TRUMP : When I first saw it, I said, “Wow! That means Vivek easily will win the race.” And then I got a call from Vivek. He said, “What would you recommend? Because I’m getting killed in the press.” “Why?” He said, “Because they think I should immediately take the ad off.” They did an ad of the mother saying the daughter is incompetent, a liar, a disgusting, unreliable person. … I said it’s a big thing. It’s like a big story about “he must take that ad down immediately. He must” — no. The mother is calling the daughter a terrible person and a liar. Everybody should be so lucky. Why would you shield somebody from that? Why would — why would we do that? So I told him, “Leave it up, and look upstairs and say, 'Thank you, God, very much. I appreciate it.'” AMY GOODMAN : The Ohio governor’s race is just one of several hotly contested races in Ohio. For more, we go to Mother Jones reporter Abby Vesoulis. Her latest piece is headlined ” GOP Doubles Down on Ad Exploiting Ohio Democrat’s Childhood Rape and Abuse.” Abby, this is an incredible story. I mean, you have a woman who contends that she was raped and sexually abused at the age of 12. And the man who did it, her stepfather, was indicted, and then he and her mother, who he was married to, fled to Pennsylvania. And Dr. Acton has not seen her mother in — what is it? — in more than 40 years, since 1978. And somehow Ramaswamy’s people found this mother, and she talks about her daughter as a liar. She last saw her when she was what? Something like 12 years old. Abby, tell us this whole story. And President Trump saying Ramaswamy called him and said, “Should I pull it down? I’m being killed on this,” and Trump said, “No, just look up and thank God”? ABBY VESOULIS : Dr. Amy Acton, the Democrat running for governor in Ohio, has previously discussed on the campaign trail and in her previous role as public health director for Ohio during COVID how she had a very rough childhood, living in tents at time, and that her stepfather sexually abused her when she was between the ages of 10 and 12. And, you know, Vivek Ramaswamy is now using that personal trauma as an effort to exploit what she went through and win this race. And he’s currently polling beneath Amy Acton, which shows, I think, that this ad is a desperate attempt to, you know, somehow pull off a victory despite poor odds. JUAN GONZÁLEZ: And, Abby, what is your sense of the reaction among the voters — not not just the political leaders, but the voters — to this ad? ABBY VESOULIS : So, I think Ohio voters are understandably upset. And what’s really interesting is that Amy Acton, among progressives, was not, you know, their favorite candidate. They were upset with some previous things she said about continuing to uphold Ohio’s laws regarding trans girls playing sports. And so, I think there were a lot of progressives who intended to not vote for Acton or sit the election out. And so, this ad, I think, is energizing those people to come to the polls and support Acton because of how despicable they feel Ramaswamy’s ad is. And among Republicans, I’ve seen Republicans say that they just cannot vote for Ramaswamy after doing this. And I think it’s important to note that a lot of Republicans — and, of course, Democrats too, but Republicans — have been very frustrated by how the Epstein files were handled by the Trump administration. And so, here you have a situation in which, you know, candidate Ramaswamy is using the sexual abuse of a child to try to win a political campaign, and given everything that has happened with Jeffrey Epstein, these people are like, “That is where I draw the line.” So, I’ve seen many Republicans say that they are either going to stay home and not vote, which will hurt all the Republicans on the ballot in Ohio — and there’s some other very close races — or that they’re not going to vote for governor, or maybe even that they’ll vote for Acton. I think this ad is bringing a lot of sympathy to her situation. AMY GOODMAN : South Carolina Republican Congressmember Nancy Mace said she was “stunned and shocked” that between the Ramaswamy ad and Republican congressmembers blocking the release of the Epstein files, quote, she said, “It’s going to take a long time for Republicans to recover from this. … We are not the party of pedophilia,” she said, unquote. And she also referenced Congressmember Max Miller. He’s running for reelection amidst accusations of domestic violence. His opponent is the Bernie Sanders-endorsed Democrat Brian Poindexter, a union iron worker. Miller’s ex-wife Emily Moreno, who’s the daughter of Ohio’s sitting Republican Senator Bernie Moreno, claims Miller burned her chest and stomach by throwing hot water at her, held a gun to her head, and claims he fractured their 2-year-old daughter’s collarbone. In August, Republican Senator Bernie Moreno called on Miller to step down, writing on social media, quote, “He should not serve in the House of Representatives. I believe Max Miller needs to seek professional help to end the clear pattern of abuse he’s left in his wake. I believe he should not be free to continue endangering others until he does,” Senator Moreno said. Earlier this month, Miller’s campaign released an ad denying the accusations of abuse against him, defending his decision to stay in the race. REP . MAX MILLER : Too many of us know the pain of divorce. It’s messy and complicated. For two years, my family’s heartbreak has been dragged onto your TV because, well, that’s politics. Despite relentless press and investigations, every allegation against me was proven false. AMY GOODMAN : Abby Vesoulis, you and your colleagues at Mother Jones obtained some 2,000 pages of court filings and police reports pertaining to Miller through public records requests. Those records also include allegations dating back to high school. Tell us what you learned about Max Miller, how voters in Ohio are responding to the revelations. We are also including the former press secretary for President Trump in his first term. Stephanie Grisham dated Max Miller and then went on to write a piece in The Washington Post that he abused her. Talk about all of this in this last few minutes we have. ABBY VESOULIS : So, what’s most important, I think, to note about the Max Miller situation is, like you said, this is a pattern of allegations. It’s not just Emily Moreno who says that Max assaulted her on multiple occasions. There’s also Stephanie Grisham, who reportedly was slapped by Miller when the two were dating during the first Trump administration. There’s also an allegation against Miller that he pushed a girl down the stairs when she was in high school because [she] denied [his] sexual advances. Politico first reported on that in 2021, when Miller was running for his first term in the House of Representatives, and they cited three witnesses who saw that exchange between Miller and the girl that he allegedly pushed down the stairs. I contacted that now woman over the summer, and she said she really didn’t want to talk about it, because it was one of the most traumatic nights of her life, even still. And so, it’s just so important to note that it’s not just Emily Moreno. And by the way, Emily Moreno’s father is a Republican senator. So, his ad, Miller’s ad, saying that this has been, you know, dredged into the news because of politics, that just doesn’t really make sense, because wouldn’t Moreno have wanted, you know, the Ohio contingency in Congress to be full of Republicans? So, there’s a lot of strange politics happening here. JUAN GONZÁLEZ: And, Abby, there’s another big race in Ohio, the Senate race, where former Senator Sherrod Brown is trying to unseat Jon Husted. What’s your sense of how that race is developing? ABBY VESOULIS : So, Sherrod Brown was senator of Ohio for 18 years before Bernie Moreno ousted him in 2024. And that was one of the closest Senate races back in 2024. And, you know, despite Ohio shifting red ever since 2016, Sherrod Brown has continued to be a fairly popular Democrat, the only Democrat in Ohio to win a statewide race in a decade-plus. And so, he has a lot of name recognition. In fact, a recent poll showed that 25% of Ohio voters thought that Sherrod Brown was still the senator and that he had never been voted out. So he has name recognition going for him. And then, additionally, because of how long he served and how fairly popular he was as a Democrat, he has a lot of campaign cash, whereas Vivek — sorry, whereas Jon Husted doesn’t have as much popularity. He’s not getting as much cash. He really doesn’t have anything to show for his two years in Congress. He hasn’t done anything notable. And so, I think the sheer amount of money Sherrod Brown has left, millions and tens of millions of dollars, and the fact that it’s considered a frontline race and Democrats are pumping a lot of money in, the polling is suggesting that Sherrod Brown is poised to win by a few points. AMY GOODMAN : Abby Vesoulis, we thank you so much for being with us, reporter for Mother Jones . We’ll link to your articles , the latest , ” GOP Doubles Down on Ad Exploiting Ohio Democrat’s Childhood Rape and Abuse.” Coming up, we go to Brazil, where Sunday’s runoff election between the right-wing Senator Flávio Bolsonaro and President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva will determine the future of the largest democracy in South America. Stay with us. [break] AMY GOODMAN : “Men Ana” by Alsarah & The Nubatones, performing in our Democracy Now! studio. To see the full performance and interview with Alsarah, go to democracynow.org. Page 2 Brazilian voters are heading to the polls on Sunday for the presidential runoff between incumbent President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva and far-right Senator Flávio Bolsonaro, with polls showing a tight race that will decide whether Brazil remains led by the left or joins the right-wing surge across Latin America. According to The Intercept Brasil , Bolsonaro’s campaign paid 600,000 Brazilian reais (about $119,000 USD ) to a U.S. company, Elytron, that specializes in election manipulation, including through online disinformation and “psychological warfare techniques” to undermine opponents. Reporter Laís Martins says that while it’s not clear whether or how the Bolsonaro campaign used Elytron’s services, it adds to suspicion of U.S. interference in the election, including Meta’s restrictions on President Lula’s social media profiles. “We’ve seen evidence pile up that something is not right, that this playing field is not equal,” says Martins. Page 3 At least 59 people have died in ICE custody since the start of President Donald Trump’s second term, the highest number in more than a decade. Many deaths have been linked to medical neglect, including four of five recent deaths at California’s Adelanto Processing Center, according to a 2026 report by the state attorney general. Al Jazeera English’s Fault Lines investigated deaths at the facility, which is operated by the private prison company GEO Group, in the new documentary Dying in Detention . “ GEO Group has made over a billion dollars in profits from immigration detention. They have given more than a million dollars … to help reelect Donald Trump,” says correspondent Natasha Del Toro. “That raises a lot of questions for us about the relationship between GEO and the federal government, and some of these conflicts of interest.”

articles.title: Israeli setrike on Iran is imminent | w/ Trita Parsi
articles.author: Zoe Alexandra
articles.content: Trita Parsi puts the odds of a new round of US-Israeli war on Iran at 90% – and it could start as soon as this weekend. The US and Israeli militaries have plans for renewed strikes after the midterms, the New York Times reports; three aircraft carriers are en route to the region, and Netanyahu, trailing ahead of Tuesday’s elections, says he’s ordered Israel’s military and Mossad to topple Iran’s government. Parsi, executive vice president of the Quincy Institute for Responsible Statecraft, tells Rania Khalek and Zoe Alexandra why Trump’s third round will be far worse than the first two. Parsi argues that Trump, initially driven by hubris, is now out for revenge against a Tehran he believes is deliberately dragging out the war to destroy his presidency. He explains why time is on Iran’s side; how Washington is spinning the war of attrition in the Strait of Hormuz; why soaring gas prices make the war impossible to tune out; and why even European conservatives say the protests sweeping the continent are fueled by the war’s economic fallout. Parsi warns Netanyahu may see escalation as the Hail Mary pass he needs to lock in his legacy, and says that if Democrats take control of Congress, they’ll have the power to stop this – and will be complicit if they don’t. Watch full episodes of BT Live, join breakthroughnews.org as a member today! #breakthroughnews ****** Rough transcript follows: [Interviewer:] It’s very difficult to see this war lead to a scenario in which the impact on the global economy is sufficiently insignificant for it not to translate to any political changes. If you look at the polls right now, the top issues motivating people in this election are inflation and gas prices. That’s all due to the Iran war. Nearly eight months ago, the US and Israel launched a very destructive war on Iran, killing the Supreme Leader and disrupting global oil markets. Trump wanted a quick knockout, but instead, he got a war he can’t contain, a stalemate that nobody seems able to break, and a deal to end it that looks further away than ever. Somehow, this war has become background noise in the US, and the next round may already be on the calendar. The New York Times reports that the US and Israeli militaries have drawn up plans for renewed strikes on Iran after the midterms. This campaign would hit energy infrastructure, nuclear sites, and Iran’s missile and drone arsenal. They came close to doing this earlier this month before Trump pulled the plug at the last minute. Now, three aircraft carriers and thousands of Marines are on the way. Netanyahu, trailing in the polls ahead of next week’s elections in Israel, says he’s ordered the military to prepare for preemptive action and to topple the regime. Iran’s intelligence assessments suggest strikes could come even before Israel votes on Tuesday. The White House says nothing happens before the midterms. Meanwhile, the State Department has ordered non-emergency staff and their families out of Saudi Arabia, and the AFP cites a diplomatic source saying families of embassy staff in the UAE, Jordan, Qatar, and Bahrain have been ordered out as well. Netanyahu is making big threats a week before elections. Trump says this time the fight will be neither quick nor limited, with no restraints. So what breaks this stalemate? Is escalation the only way out? And who can last longer, Iran or Washington? Joining us now to discuss all of this is Trita Parsi, executive vice president of the Quincy Institute. Trita, welcome back to BT Live. [Trita Parsi:] Good to be with you. [Interviewer:] You are putting the odds of a new round of war at 90%. That’s quite high. The New York Times says the plans are drawn up and carriers are on their way. Why are you and the New York Times so confident? Some US planners think that three days of intense strikes will manage to break Iran’s economy and force concessions. Is that a serious theory? [Trita Parsi:] First of all, it’s kind of insulting to say that the New York Times and I are on the same page on this. I’m just kidding. But look, I’ve been warning about this for more than five weeks now that a third round was extremely likely because of a couple of factors. What we’re seeing now is more the motions necessary to bring about this disastrous third round being put in place. The signs and the logic as to why we were going in this direction were clear to me several weeks ago because Trump, at the end of the day, his psychology does not allow for him to lose. He is willing to sacrifice everything to win. Earlier on, he thought that the MOU and a diplomatic deal could end the story in a way that made the war look worth it or at least acceptable. But he had a bad experience with the MOU. He got attacked for it by Democrats, Republicans, the pro-Israel crowd, everyone. He realized the political cost was very high. So now he thinks diplomacy won’t end it acceptably. Blockade won’t end it acceptably, even though they’re putting forward this mythology that they’re winning on the blockade. And the limited amount of war he’s had won’t do it. So now the only thing he hasn’t tried is this all-out war that he threatened several times but never did—taking out Iran’s oil infrastructure, energy infrastructure, desalination plants, critical infrastructure. He avoided that, knowing it would lead to massive retaliation by the Iranians against GCC infrastructure, which would throw the global economy into a depression. But now he doesn’t seem to care. The midterms are over, and he’s just looking to do something that brings this to an end on his terms. There’s another element that makes matters worse now, which is last time he went in with hubris. He thought he could do this in four days. The Israelis had sold him that mythology. He had managed to do Venezuela quickly, so he was very confident. This time, it’s not hubris bringing him back; it’s vindictiveness. He’s very angry about the war’s outcome so far. He believes the Iranians deliberately dragged things out to destroy his presidency, and to a certain extent, they have. Now there’s this new element of revenge. So we may very well go towards a third disastrous round of war, not because of a flawed geopolitical miscalculation, but because of one man’s desire for vengeance. [Interviewer:] It’s truly tanking the global economy, putting tens of thousands of lives at risk because of vengeance. Trump has previously vetoed a major return to combat, including at the last minute earlier this month. He’s pulled back from major threats repeatedly. The White House says no strikes before midterms. Iran’s intelligence says it could come before Israel votes on Tuesday. Which clock is correct? If the Republicans lose Congress, can Democrats stop a possible escalation? Will they? [Trita Parsi:] Unfortunately, not to the extent that they should be. It’s perhaps a different political calculation before the midterms versus after. But with the MOU, there were Democrats who should have known better, who played a fantastic role in the JCPOA, who now returned a favor to the Republicans by doing bad faith attacks against the MOU. It contributed to the MOU collapsing. It’s not the only reason, but it contributed to Trump’s conception that a deal with Iran is not a win because of the high political price, a conception every previous American president has had. It’s interesting that Trump didn’t have it. It’s part of why he was willing to strike a deal with Iran, willing to strike a deal with North Korea because he was immune to the idea of a political cost for such an agreement. But that’s changed, and the Democrats contributed to it. After the midterms, it will be critical for Democrats to do everything they can, from using the power of the purse to other means, to put an end to this war. Once they’re in control of the House and particularly if they also control the Senate, they’re no longer bystanders. They’re complicit if this is allowed to continue because they will have the power to stop it. [Interviewer:] There’s so much damage incurred from this war, obviously not as much as the Iranian side, but it still stands to be seen just how deep that damage can go. Iranian officials are now talking about expanding targets to data centers and undersea internet cables. Iran analysts floated hitting Saudi refineries like Aramco to spike oil prices. A top adviser to Ghalibaf called the idea of that 72-hour war a fantasy. What does the next round look like from Iran’s side? How much more can they escalate? Why do you think Iran has decided to wait out Trump rather than cut any more deals? [Trita Parsi:] I spoke to a senior advisor to a European president who’s no longer in office, not particularly unsympathetic to Trump. I asked him about the protests around Europe, not just in France, but in many other countries. How much of that is driven by the economic consequences of this war? To my surprise, he said overwhelmingly, a lot of it has to do with the economic consequences of this war. The focus is often on immigration, but it’s not the driving force. Even someone from the right, more on the anti-immigrant side, said what we’re seeing in Europe is largely driven by the economic consequences of this war. The global repercussions so far, in the first two rounds, are going to be benign compared to the third round, which will become overwhelming. The other part of your question, if you could repeat? [Interviewer:] I was wondering why Iran has decided to wait out Trump rather than cut any more deals. [Trita Parsi:] That’s a very good question. In this war of attrition, the Iranians have been comfortable—not in the sense that they’re not hurting, but because they believe time is on their side. The Trump administration is putting forward a different story, saying they’re winning. They won the battle of Hormuz, more volume is coming out of the Strait of Hormuz, and they’re winning the war of attrition. Yet, it’s the US and Israel about to start this war, which tells you something about who actually is winning that war of attrition. The administration has been successful not because of their brilliance but because of the lack of brilliance in the media and analytical core. They said focus only on the volume of oil coming out, not the cost or oil prices. The impression was that the war of attrition is being won by the American side, and if anyone wanted to escalate, it would have been the Iranians. But reality seems to be the opposite. Israel goes to vote on October 27th. If Netanyahu loses, he’ll be a caretaker, and technically, it would be hard for him to launch a war. Some analysts think he could use the threat of an imminent strike to force his rivals into a unity government. Are these threats about Iran or about keeping his job, or is that essentially the same? [Trita Parsi:] I think they’re pretty much one and the same. I’m not convinced that being a caretaker would make it more difficult for him to start. There will be resistance from within the security establishment, but the resistance may be higher because they’re worried he’ll start this war to impact the elections or force their postponement. The chief of staff of the army has publicly said this. Once the elections are over, and it’s in the process of forming a coalition, I’m not convinced he won’t have the ability to start a war, and certainly not convinced he wouldn’t want to. If he feels he’s about to lose the coalition, this would be his last chance for his legacy to do what his secretary of defense said is the Israeli objective: bomb Iran back to the stone age, shift the balance of power in the region so dramatically that Israel will no longer have a problem with Iran providing any deterrence against Israel. That has been the Israeli objective, and the Israelis are so openly talking about it, yet it almost never translates to any real conversation in Washington. [Interviewer:] Lastly, before we let you go, this war has really fallen off the front page. It’s become so normalized, like background noise. Do you think there’s a risk that opposition to this war fades because it’s becoming a kind of forever war that people just tune out, or is it too damaging to the global economy to stay a forever war? [Trita Parsi:] Part of the reason the US could have forever wars was because the political cost of ending the war was higher than the political cost of continuing a losing war, which was because the cost of continuing the war was relatively low. In Afghanistan, it was not good, but as long as casualties were low, the anger never reached a critical mass. The wars in Iraq and Afghanistan had no significant impact on the economy or oil markets in the manner that this war has had. It’s difficult to see this war lead to a scenario where the impact on the global economy is insignificant enough not to translate to political changes. If you look at the polls, the top issues motivating people in this election are inflation and gas prices, all due to the Iran war. Corruption ranks even higher, but both sides believe the other is corrupt, whereas with the Iran war, there’s no debate about who started it and why. The risk of escalation is far greater than the opportunities for de-escalation, which does not lend itself to an endless, low-intensity war that just continues. It could be a long war with highs and lows, still costly, but not just simmering in the background. [Interviewer:] Real quick, put a number on it. You believe there’s going to be another round starting this weekend. Since you like percentages, put a percentage on it. [Trita Parsi:] I put it at 90%. It could only change if Trump changes his mind. He’s been on the point of approving something and changed his mind seven times. We can’t have a situation like this continue without him agreeing at some point. That’s why the odds are the way they are. He’s not going to constantly back off last minute. At some point, he’s going to say yes, go through with it, and all of us are going to pay the price for it. [Interviewer:] Trita Parsi, executive vice president of the Quincy Institute, always appreciate your analysis. Thank you so much for joining us. [Trita Parsi:] Thank you so much. Appreciate it.
